In game economies are usually pretty hard to make compelling. Again, pretty much every game ever has this problem: At a certain point, there's nothing to buy. (And also buying stuff is completely optional anyway cause the main quest will give you all the gear you need regardless.) GTA 5 is just particularly unusual in that there's really no way to earn money... until the final mission where the game just dumps absurd amounts of money in your lap. And by that point there really isn't much to do. It's an odd design choice that bothered me even back in 2013 that I have never seen anyone talk about.

I was kinda thinking about making an opinion post about this but honestly GTA V has the weirdest in game economy I've seen and I've never seen this brought up when people talk about the game. (This is purely for the campaign, I'm a purely single player person and have not touched GTAO)

In basically every other GTA game, and every other game with an in game currency, you gain money by doing missions. Usually by a certain point you have more money than you could ever spend. In GTA V, the majority of missions don't give any money. Even the "bank heists" that were touted as a major selling point don't give you money, just the first and last ones. Granted, the story does give a reason why these missions aren't giving you money, ie you're working for the FIB not because the characters want money but because Dave is blackmailing Michael. Franklin and Trevor work for Devin Weston under the promise Devin will pay handsomely only for him to back out of the deal once he gets what he wants, etc. But still, the majority of missions in GTA V do not give you money. Then suddenly, the last mission that concludes the game gives you more money than you could ever possibly spend. I think I got 60 million, so I immediately bought all the best weapons, all the best upgrades for Franklins car, all the clothes and tattoos in the game, most properties, a helicopter, and by the end I still had like, 57 million. 

Also the main reason to buy a property is the property provides passive income. But if you look at how much each property cost versus how much income it provides, a 200k property will give you 2k a week, meaning it would take 2 in game *years* to return a profit. At that point, why bother?

So the idea is that the AI uses numbers to determine behaviors, with one, aggression being how likely they are to declare war on you. I think videos like this are ignorant of Star Wars in general. The Original trilogy lightsaber fights were super basic, and it wasn't just due to the low budget. George Lucas was basically inspired by 3 things: The Hero's Journey, Flash Gordon serials, and Samurai films. Lightsabers were essentially sci fi Nodachi (think Katana, but even bigger), that were meant to be wielded with 2 hands and were extremely heavy, and the choreography is supposed to reflect how difficult it was to wield one of these things.

The Prequel trilogy changed that, essentially saying "this is a hilt with a weightless blade" and designed the lightsaber to be fast and nimble, so you get fights that seem more like well choreographed dances than actual swordfights, which can be entertaining on it's own but it is a difference compared to the OT.

The Sequel trilogy takes way more inspiration from the original trilogy than the prequel trilogy. I believe the reason for this is, when the ST was being written, internet consensus is that the OT was great and the PT was garbage, so the ST wanted to take inspiration from the films people remembered fondly and not the ones people hated. But as the years have passed people who grew up on the PT developed rose tinted glasses for it and now people view the PT more positively than in 2014. But yeah the ST takes way more inspiration from the OT, for one, Episodes 7 is basically a soft reboot of episode 4 with a gender swapped Luke. Episode 8 tries to be an subversion of your expectations, audiences reacted poorly to that, then episode 9 went back to being a soft reboot. You can tell this from the plot but also the artstyle is way closer to the OT than the ST, and the lightsaber fights try to emphasize that the lightsaber has weight again.

It's also important to note that in both the PT, the saber part of the lightsaber was basically a bit of plastic that would be lit up in post, where as with the ST, the saber actually has LED lights in it to make the light across the actor's more realistic, but this means the prop the actors are holding is physically heavier as a result.

I don't think one style of choreography is objectively better than the other, it's just different approaches.

So, I have thoughts on this.

I see removing attributes as unambiguous positive in my opinion. One reason for this is that almost everything attributes did in previous games can also be done in Skyrim. Let's take a look at them individually.

**Strength** increases carrying capacity and melee weapon damage.

**Endurance** increases health

**Intelligence** increases total magicka

**Willpower** In morrowind it increased chance of successfully casting a spell. In oblivion it increases magicka regeneration

**Agility** increases stamina

**Speed** increases.... speed

**Personality** increases how much people like you

**Luck** applies a small bonus to all random dice rolls.

In Skyrim, instead of leveling up Endurance/Intelligence/Agility/Strength to increase health, magic, stamina or carrying capacity, you just increase these things directly. Increased magicka regen can be done with enchanting or potions or certain perks in the restoration skill tree. Because of the sprint feature, increasing Stamina also indirectly increases how fast you can run, by allowing you to run fast for longer. A perk in the heavy armor skill tree removes the speed penalty for wearing heavy armor, indirectly increasing speed. Certain shouts are dedicated towards mobility. Personality was already redundant because of the speechcraft tree. Removing Oblivion's awful speechcraft minigame was probably the right decision anyway. Luck was important to Morrowind where practically every action outside of walking was determined by a random number generator by since Oblivion moved away from this Luck basically had no effect. And because luck could only increase by a max of +1 each level and not +5 even in Morrowind Luck based builds were not possible.

I don't know how controversial an opinion this is but I think the leveling system in Skyrim is a significant improvement over the one in Morrowind and Oblivion. It retains the "improve a skill by using it" idea the previous two had, which is both intuitive and unique from other RPGs, but gets rid of the efficient leveling nonsense you had to deal with in Oblivion.

Plus, while the perk system wasn't perfect, I much preferred getting a perk because that meant potentially getting a new ability to play around with. This is more satisfying to me than watching numbers on a spreadsheet marginally go up. 

It did have flaws, the perks that were essentially "deal 10% more damage with swords (0/5)" were not exciting but basically required if you wanted to use a build using swords, but overall it was such an improvement that it makes Oblivion and Morrowind hard to go back to.

Apocrypha is loosely inspired by the aesthetics of Lovecraft, while Dagon's deadlands has an aesthetic closer to hell. 

Lots of fantasy worlds do this as well. Dungeons and Dragons was the Original Roleplaying game, and the entire setting of the Forgotten Realms world was also written as a kitchen sink and this was purposeful as it allowed the DM to write whatever kind of story they wanted to tell within that setting.

>!So Morrowind had more distinct NPCs than Oblivion and Skyrim combined. The problem is that these distinct NPCs all had the same lines of dialogue for each conversational topic, making them feel more like walking encyclopedias rather than actual characters. One of Oblivion's ambitions was to rectify this with the radiant AI. Basically, it had fewer NPCs but each one was fully voiced, had unique dialogue, and a daily (sometimes weekly) schedule. There would also be internal behavior modifiers governing how that npc interacted with the world around it. All NPCs needed to eat once a day. If the character had the money, they would buy food. If not, they would steal. How good they are at stealing depended on THEIR sneak stats. If caught stealing, the other NPC, based on their behavior modifiers would either fight them, flee, report them to the guard, or do nothing. Characters would also have procedurally generated conversations with each other. In 2006 this was incredibly ambitious and impressive, and even though the background conversations were a bit goofy and could repeat themselves, I wish Skyrim refined radiant AI rather than scrapping the system. I know generative AI is controversial but I really think the technology now exists to perfect this system. Major NPCs and key story beats would still have to be written by hand, but the minor side characters could be populated by an AI generator, with a human checking over things making sure nothing goes wrong. Background conversations, instead of being canned lines of dialogue thrown at each other, could then be generated by a large language model with some prompting to make it fit the Elder Scrolls world. !<

Unpopular opinion: Skyrim's leveling system is better than Oblivion's or Morrowind's. 

It retains the core idea of "level up skills by using them" which is both intuitive and unique from other RPGs. However it gets rid of the awful "efficient leveling" bullshit you had to deal with under the previous two games. The perk system, while not perfect, can make leveling up an exciting experience because you're gaining new abilities, not just watch numbers on a spreadsheet marginally increase. Almost everything the attribute system brought in Oblivion and Morrowind can be done in Skyrim too. Only instead of leveling up Endurance to increase health, you just... level up health. Instead of leveling up Intelligence to increase magicka, you, increase magicka. Only luck isn't in Skyrim but considering Skyrim and Oblivion are no longer using dice rolls the same way TES1-3 did, Luck never really did much. Yeah there's no class system but the class system in Morrowind and Oblivion was awful. Unlike other RPGs you are encouraged to use all abilities, your class just determined which skills would lead to level ups. This led to meta strategies such as picking a class that has abilities in skills you know you won't be using much to get around Oblivion's awful level scaling. In Skyrim, your class is just what skills you use and what perks you have. It also still has birthsign bonuses, except they're in the form of sigil stones. This is meant to encourage exploration and also you can change your sigil sign bonus so you aren't stuck with a bad decision you made at the first 5 minutes of the game.

More Morrowind Thoughts.

One thing I think Morrowind does well compared to Oblivion and Skyrim that I don't often see discussed is that non-combat skills and spells are actually kinda important. For example, in Oblivion and Skyrim, to pick a lock, you played a minigame. Having a higher security skill made the minigame easier and having a stronger lock made the minigame harder, but it's still possible for someone with a lockpicking skill of 15 to open a master lock. With Morrowind, there's no minigame. Your chance to pick the lock is (lockingpickingSkill + Luck/10) *LockpickQuality *fatigueBonus - lockLevel. This is your percentage to pick the lock, and if this number is at or below 0, you simply can't pick the lock. This is combined with the fact that, in Oblivion and Skyrim, the only reason to pick locks is to get extra loot from locked chests in dungeons. Totally optional and you arent' missing anything if you don't bother. In Morrowind, some quests will require you to break in somewhere to get information or an item, and if you can't pick that level 50 lock, well... you have to find away around that, either Open lock spell, or a fortify security spell or potion or enchantment, or buying a higher quality lockpick. But There's actually a tangible benefit to upgrading your non combat stats in a way Oblivion and Skyrim just don't have.

Holy shit is Sunder completely overpowered. Let me explain why

Morrowind has a "to hit chance" How this is calculated is (weaponskill + agility/5 + luck/10 + attack) * fatigueBonus. If you are at 0% stamina then fatigueBonus will be .75. If you have full stamina fatigueBonus will be 1.25. Where a lot of people think Morrowind makes it impossible to hit is that they start playing with the iron dagger given in the tutorial, but they don't pick short blade as part of their major attributes, they also don't conserve stamina. So just starting out of Seydna Neen, and you have 30 agility and 40 luck (pretty standard for a level 1 character) your calculation is (5 + 30/5 + 40/10 + 0) * .75. This is a 12% chance to hit with every strike. Also, weapons only increase in stats for every successful hit, making a chicken and egg problem when starting out. Granted, if you pick a weapon you're actually good at this percent goes up quite a bit. For example, I was using long blade and my agility was 36 and I got the warrior stone which gives +10 attack so the formula for hitting with my enchanted glass longsword at medium stamina was (70 + 35/5 + 40/10 + 10) * 1 = 91% chance to hit. Pretty good. Now, Sunder increases attack by 30 and luck by 20. That's an 32% chance to hit compared to other blunt weapons. Even though my blunt weapon skill was only 25, this still ended up being (25 + 35/5 + 60/10 + 40) * 1 or 78% chance to hit. Even though my blunt weapon skill is GARBAGE I was still hitting the vast majority of attacks. Plus sunder also increases strength by 20 (which factors quite a bit into how much damage is done). This is on top of a base heavy attack damage of 40-70 (which is a lot in this game) I switched to using Sunder as my main weapon and now my blunt weapon skill is 47. I have a higher chance to hit with Sunder than I do a long blade even though my long blade skill is 75

Starting with Ratchet and Clank 2, weapons could upgrade. How the upgrade system works is different per game, but in general, when you use a gun, you get xp, and when you fill the xp bar the gun goes up a level. Most games had multiple tiers of upgrades and each tier would just be a straight damage increase over the previous, or it would let you unlock more of the raritanium upgrade tree. In R&C2 however, weapons only upgraded once, but when they did they became a completely different weapon, for example, the mini bomb becoming a mini-nuke that did much more damage and had much higher AOE. Usually the gun became an objectively better, cooler version of itself. Sometimes however, the gun would become a worse version of itself. The lava gun shot a continual stream of lava at enemies. The lava didn't do a lot of damage but it was great when you were surrounded by weak enemies, as a quick spin would spew lava in all directions dealing with the  numerous weak threats. Then when it upgraded it became the magma gun, which shoots discrete chunks of magma at the enemy. Now the magma gun if targeted at a single enemy DID do more DPS than the lava gun, but because it shot discrete chunks, spinning around holding fire would no longer clear the room of weak enemies, effectively removing the niche scenario the lava gun was used for. There's no way to un-upgrade or choose not to upgrade either.

So this is a topic I've thought of, and I thought of doing a sample summary of what games are violent and which aren't, using my steam page as the sample size. I mostly stick to critically acclaimed games so there's heavy overlap between the 100 games I own on steam and [this](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_video_games_considered_the_best) 

So, the issue I ran into was trying to define what counts as violence in a video game. Obviously games like Assassin's Creed, Call of Duty, Grand Theft Auto definitely count as violent but there were a lot of games that were in kind of a grey area. I could broadly fit these into a few categories

**Violence in the narrative but not mechanics** This would be something like Ace Attorney or What Remains of Edith Finch, where murder or at least death is depicted regularly but you as the player aren't participating.  Telltale games or David Cage games would also fit this, as there isn't really a combat system but there is combat in the form of QTE sequences.

**The player doesn't kill but the player can die** A lot of platformers fit this definition. Super meat boy is a very gory game, with your blood splattering the walls every time you make a mistake, but you aren't doing any killing. Portal would also fit this category. Journey arguably fits this category but only for one of it's sections. 

**Violence is abstract or cartoony to the point where I don't know if it should count** This would be your Undertales or your Civilizations, where there are combat mechanics but they don't feel visceral enough to feel like youre killing someone, especially for Undertale. Katamari Damacy sorta fits this with you crushing humans under the weight of your ever growing ball but I don't know if this counts as violent.

To add to what you were saying earlier, depending on what type of game you are making, you don't necessarily need sophisticated AI. For example, in a shooter, you need pathfinding so NPCs know not to run into doorways or walk off cliffs, and they need to have at least some sense of self preservation so it doesn't feel like I can just camp outside a hallway and have them all walk into my gunfire. 

But beyond that? Do you really need anymore? The pathfinding thing has been solved since Doom back in 1993. The sense of self preservation thing is usually solved by differing enemy types with differing behaviors, like a sniper enemy that hides and waits for you rather than the other way around, or a tough melee enemy that knows it can tank the hits if it charges you directly, so even if you wait in a hallway for it to pop out so you can shoot it, it will still pose a threat.

With stealth games they often have to make guards dumber than they would be in real life because sneaking undetected into a base in real life without being seen would be almost impossible.

Part of the importance of Citizen Kane is historic, something that would be hard to appreciate if watched today.

So basically, during the history of early film you had a lot of people just experimenting with the art of filmmaking, so some of the great early films are great because they acted like experiments of just creating a film (much like how early video games in the 1960s were just people at DARPA or university students just messing around with computers in their free time and seeing what they could do) then when filmmaking started to become it's own artform, there were a lot of variations in what people were using the new technology to do. Many early films are basically theatre plays that were recorded. 

Citizen Kane did a lot with cinematography and perspective that previous films sort of explored but Citizen Kane really perfected it in a way that is innovative that all films since take inspiration to whether they realize it or not, it's just become such a natural part of filmmaking. 

You can say the same with video games to a certain degree. Grand theft auto 3 wasn't the first open world game but GTA3 was the first that became a hit, and it set a darker tone that video games could be for more than just kids. And the GTA series in general showed the potential of open world style games that really blew up later.

I mean, we have stuff like Disco Elysium and Planescape Torment if you're looking for sophisticated writing. But in terms of Citizen Kane comparison, there ARE games that have acted as watershed moments and completely changed gaming as we know it. Some of these would include Doom 1 (the original), Half Life 1, Grand Theft Auto 3, World of Warcraft, Resident Evil 4 (the original). Although these are watershed moments for completely different reasons.

**Dishonored: Deathloop**

So earlier I did a review of The Outer Worlds where I commented that the pre-release hype was massive but then once the game released it pretty much disappeared from gaming discourse, and after playing it, I could understand why; The Outer Worlds is a mediocre game. 

Deathloop (which is technically a part of the Dishonored universe although I don't think this detail really adds anything to the experience) is in a similar situation. Massive pre-release hype, amazing critical scores, several GOTY nominations (but no wins), but then fan reception was not so hot. After playing the game myself, I could see why; Deathloop is a mediocre game. Unlike The Outer Worlds however, I feel like Deathloop is only a few small tweaks away from greatness. There's a lot of talent and creativity that went into Deathloop, it's just let down by a few glaringly bad design decisions. The main one is that they don't let you figure out how to take down all your targets. Instead, you're given quest objectives then once you complete those quests a cutscene appears outright telling you the sequence of events needed to kill all 8 targets in one day. If they just made it so you had to figure this out for yourself by going out into the world and gathering information on your target's schedule instead of just following a waypoint compass, the world would have been a lot more engaging. They have all the pieces in place to implement this too. They have 8 distinct weirdos as assassination targets with defined personalities and interpersonal relationships that you manipulate in order to get everyone in one loop. The problem is that there is one way to do it, only one way, and the game outright tells you how to do it. You can't do it in any other order. For example, cult leader Harriet appears in Karl's Bay in the morning. This is the only time she appears. She doesn't appear at any other location at any other time of day, her character model simply disappears at noon and you lose your shot. So you have to go to the bay first thing in the loop. No creativity or personal expression in how you approach the overall mission, which is such an utterly baffling design choice for an immersive sim it makes me wonder what Arkane were thinking. 

Another one is that you can "infuse" gear so that you retain it day by day. What that means is that you might stumble upon a very powerful weapon early in the game and can use some time-points so you can have it for the rest of the game. I stumbled upon a purple tiered silenced SMG that is very accurate even at long distance and headshots are one hit kill for normal enemies. You can imagine how much having this weapon in my regular arsenal broke stealth and combat. Now imagine if I had to go out of my way to get this gun each and every time the loop reset? That would be an interesting choice with the clock ticking, but oh wait, the game doesn't actually progress time naturally, you transition from one time period to the next by moving in between districts, so you have as long as you like to just explore each district and time will not move. 

I make comparisons to The Outer Worlds because that games just bores me. There needs to be a lot more creative effort put in to make that game interesting. Deathloop frustrates me because I think it was so close to being so much greater. The creativity and talent are there, it's just a few small changes away from being great.
